## Chapter Summary

A business intelligence tool serves readers who want to ask the next question themselves. Power BI Desktop, a free Windows application, is where a report is built: data is loaded and prepared with Power Query, the tables are related in a semantic model, and interactive visuals are laid out on report pages. The Power BI service is where reports are published, shared, and read in a browser, and where dashboards, single pages of tiles pinned from reports, can be built. Most Excel features of Part II have a Power BI counterpart. A matrix visual plays the part of a PivotTable, a slicer filters every visual on its page, and a relationship between tables does the work of a merge.

Power BI reads the Charles River Tables of CharlesRiver.xlsx through Get data and the Navigator, and the Power Query Editor shapes them with the steps of Chapters 4 and 5 before Close & Apply loads them into the model. The editor's column quality, distribution, and profile describe each column, but by default they describe only the first 1,000 rows. For the invoice lines, those rows predate every promotion, so a profile of the sample suggests that no line ever carried one. The profile becomes reliable only when it is switched to the entire data set. Two defaults are turned off at the start of a report: Auto date/time, which adds hidden date tables, and the autodetection of relationships, which guesses keys from column names.

The tables of a model stay separate and are joined by relationships, which Power BI cannot read from the Charles River database because its foreign keys are not declared. Most relationships are one-to-many, and a filter flows from the one side to the many side, so a selection on Item reaches the invoice lines but not the invoices. A model is reconciled before it is used. The Validation page of the tutorials reproduces the invoice line count and the line total of Chapter 6 to the cent, and shows no item group as (Blank).

A visual summarizes whatever is placed in its value wells, which creates an implicit measure. Its defaults sum keys, codes, and years, count lines when invoices are meant, and average rates line by line, so key and year columns are set to Don't summarize, invoices are counted with a distinct count on the lines, and ratios wait for the measures of Chapter 14. Cards, charts, matrices, and slicers make up a report page, and clicking a data point filters or highlights the other visuals on the page. Edit interactions changes that behavior, and a filter that changes the meaning of a number belongs where the reader can see it, not hidden in the Filters pane.

An honest visual matches its encoding to its reader's task. Position along a common scale is read more accurately than angle, area, or shading, and graphs suit questions about patterns while tables suit questions about exact values. Three choices often mislead with correct numbers. A line chart's axis fitted to the data magnifies small changes, a second value axis on a combo chart invites comparisons between scales that mean nothing, and a comparison that starts at an unusual period, such as Charles River's start-up month of January 2024, overstates growth. An accessible report gives text enough contrast, never lets color carry meaning alone, describes every visual in its alternative text, and uses a consistent theme.
